background.definition: Mesenteric adenitis is the presence of enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes in patient who presents with abdominal pain consistent with appendicitis but who is identified as having a normal appendix.

list.listitem: In 2 studies, mesenteric adenitis was the discharge diagnosis in 7.7% and 8.3% of patients with an admission diagnosis of appendicitis.
Mesenteric adenitis is frequently infectious, most often viral, including rotavirus but also Yersinia enterocolitica, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, Campylobacter, and nontypeable Salmonella.
Mesenteric adenitis and terminal ileitis is associated with Yersinia infection.
Mesenteric adenitis can also be secondary to other inflammatory conditions in the abdomen, including inflammatory bowel disease, pancreatitis, and appendicitis.
Infection or an inflammatory bowel condition leads to mesenteric adenopathy.
This in turn leads to right lower quadrant pain that may mimic appendicitis.
Mesenteric adenitis frequently presents as a pseudoappendicitis syndrome. C

Diagnosis is made by ruling out appendicitis (through imaging where appropriate) and by the visualization of a cluster of 3 or more mesenteric lymph nodes with a short-axis diameter of greater than 5 mm. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Identification on CT or US of appendix with diameter greater than 6 mm
Bloody diarrhea more common with Yersinia infections
Usually a more insidious onset; diagnosis frequently can be made on colonoscopy

list.listitem: Patients with mesenteric adenitis often present as a pseudoappendicitis syndrome and are often only diagnosed after negative laparotomy.

Compared with patients with nonruptured appendicitis, those with mesenteric adenitis were less likely to have right lower quadrant tenderness (75% vs 91%) and rebound tenderness (48% vs 68%). There was no difference with respect to rectal tenderness or the presence of bowel sounds.

In studies in the United States with sporadic and outbreak-associated Yersinia infections, abdominal pain was present in 86% to 97% of patients, diarrhea in 47% to 100%, bloody diarrhea in 20% to 60%, fever in 77% to 100%, and vomiting in 27% to 48%.

The mean WBC in patients with nonperforated appendicitis was 15,570 (range 10,300-20,840), compared to 12,470 (range 7370-17,570) in patients with mesenteric adenitis. CRP and ESR may be higher than in patients with appendicitis. But these test results can also be quite elevated in patients with appendicitis.

The CT appearance of the abdominal nodes in mesenteric adenitis and acute appendicitis can be identical. The presence of a nodes in the small bowel mesentery suggests mesenteric adenitis as the etiology. Thickening of the wall of the ileum and cecum can be seen in both conditions; significant thickening raises the question of Crohn's disease as the etiology for the mesenteric adenopathy.

The ability of CT to demonstrate pathology other than appendicitis (eg, mesenteric adenitis) depends on technique; scans focused on the lower abdomen and done without contrast (IV, oral, rectal) will reduce the likelihood of detecting other pathology.

Graded compression abdominal ultrasound is also an effective imaging modality, with the diagnosis of mesenteric adenitis established by nonvisualization of an inflamed appendix, visualization of an inflamed terminal ileum, and visualization of enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. However, the thickened terminal ileum may be confused with an inflamed appendix. Nonvisualization of an inflamed appendix may be a false negative finding.
Point of care ultrasound can identify mesenteric adenitis in children.
MRI has greater overall accuracy than ultrasound in pregnant women, but contrast should be used judiciously if needed and avoided entirely in the first trimester.

Presentation is frequently that of an acute-onset abdominal pain and may be indistinguishable from acute appendicitis, including localization to the right lower quadrant. The general diagnostic approach should be the same as for any patient presenting with acute abdominal pain.
Visualization of a normal appendix and a cluster of 3 or more mesenteric lymph nodes with a short-axis diameter greater than 5 mm reliably establishes the diagnosis of mesenteric adenitis.
The diagnostic performance of ultrasonography (US) is highly operator dependent but avoids radiation exposure. MRI may be useful in pregnant patients in whom US is inconclusive.
The timespan for recovery in children <16 years old is approximately 4 weeks. Half of patients will have symptoms for 3-10 weeks.
Supportive therapy is sufficient in most cases. C

Consider antibiotic therapy in the toxic, immunocompromised, or very young patient. Fluoroquinolones are effective empirical therapy in patients who are severely ill or have bacterial pathogens, but resistance to Campylobacter may develop during therapy. A
Treatment of Yersinia infections does not shorten the duration of illness, although it may shorten the duration of shedding of the organism. However, person-to-person transmission is rare.

Patients who appear toxic, have bloody diarrhea, or who are immunocompromised or very young may benefit from antibiotic therapy. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, aminoglycosides, piperacillin, third-generation cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones are generally effective in Yersinia infections; penicillin and first-generation cephalosporins are not.

Antibiotic treatment of Campylobacter infections may shorten the duration of illness, but because of concern about the development of resistance, caution is advised in their use in uncomplicated cases. Erythromycin is the drug of choice; increasing rates of fluoroquinolone resistance is seen, perhaps because of the use of fluoroquinolones as a poultry feed additive. Aminoglycosides are also effective, but organisms show resistance to beta lactams, cotrimoxazole, metronidazole, and tetracycline.
For those with mild illness from nontypeable Salmonella, there is no benefit from antimicrobial treatment.
Caution should be taken giving antibiotics to patients suspected of having toxigenic E. coli, as there may be a risk of increasing the incidence of hemolytic-uremic syndrome.

Surgery does not have a place in the treatment of mesenteric adenitis, although there are patients for whom a firm clinical diagnosis cannot be made and laparotomy will be necessary to rule out appendicitis.
Mesenteric adenitis is usually self-limited, so supportive therapy with fluids and analgesics is all that is required in most cases.
Consider hospitalizing patients with high fever or severe diarrhea.
Prognosis is good from the initial infection. C
Postinfection syndromes, including arthritis, are seen in some patients. C
